title: Spiral key to Universe's expansion
caption: The spiral galaxy NGC 5584, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: NGC 5584 · constellation Virgo · about 70 million light-years away (source figure)
credit: NASA, ESA, A. Riess (STScI/JHU), L. Macri (Texas A & M University), and the Hubble Heritage Team (STScI/AURA)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: This Hubble view shows the spiral galaxy NGC 5584, in the constellation of Virgo. It played a key part in a study that measured how fast the Universe is expanding more precisely than ever before.

Hubble resolves the galaxy into thousands of separate stars. Some of them are Cepheids, bright stars that pulse in brightness. Once you know how long a Cepheid takes to brighten and fade, you can work out its true brightness. Comparing that with how bright it looks reveals its distance, the most accurate way to measure distances to most nearby galaxies.

A team led by Adam Riess used Cepheids in several galaxies to pin down the expansion rate, known as Hubble's constant, to an accuracy of 3.3 percent. NGC 5584 also recently hosted a Type Ia supernova, a kind of explosion used to measure the far Universe, making it a valuable link between the two distance scales.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.34 x 2.66 arcminutes) and distance (70 million light years), the frame spans roughly 48,000 × 54,000 light-years. Its light set out about 70 million years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: This composite comes from Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3. Light through a filter passing most visible light is shown in white, a yellow-green filter in blue, and near-infrared light in red.
understand.eye: Hours of exposure reveal thousands of individual stars no eye could separate, and part of the data is near-infrared light we cannot see.

explore: The galaxy was first spotted as a faint glow by the visual observer E. E. Barnard in 1881, using only a 12.5-cm telescope.
The image was built from many exposures totalling 20.8 hours, and covers a field 2.4 arcminutes across.
alt: A spiral galaxy resolved into thousands of stars.
